title: How French Theory Lost Its Cool
author: Geoff Shullenberger
content:
![How French Theory Lost Its
Cool](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/07/GettyImages-1643656639.jpg)

> _The Frenchmen: or, My Life in Theory_  
>  By Emily Eakin  
> Penguin Press, 471 pages, $35

Jean-Luc Godard called the French generation of the 1960s "the children of
Marx and Coca Cola"; for my part, I am in some sense a child of French Theory.
When I was a babbling baby, my graduate student mother wrote a poem
chronicling my first efforts at speech laced with allusions to the ideas of
Jacques Lacan; around that time, my father was finishing up a dissertation on
the poetry of John Milton, under the heavy influence of Jacques Derrida. My
parents' infatuation with these thinkers wasn't unusual: Their ideas were in
the air people breathed in humanities academia at the time. Before I was
conscious, I was inhaling it second-hand.

The result is that my relation to French Theory--that cluster of imported
ideas associated with figures like Lacan, Derrida, and Michel Foucault--isn't
entirely unlike, or separable from, my relation to my family. In both cases,
periods of estrangement and rebellion have alternated with periods of renewed
appreciation; I find their idiosyncrasies endearing and exasperating in
roughly equal measure, and the only thing more irritating to me than their
all-too-familiar foibles is an ill-informed attack from an outsider. When it
comes to theory, there have been plenty of those.

I therefore felt a kinship with Emily Eakin as I read her new book _The
Frenchmen: or, My Life in Theory_. An entertaining hybrid of autobiography and
intellectual history, it is outstanding not just for its lucid expositions of
challenging ideas but for conveying viscerally what the encounter with them
felt like in the early years of their stateside reception. "Theory was a
symbol," as Eakin recalls, "of intellectual nonconformism, a badge, like a
pink mohawk, that marked you as a member of the counterculture, different from
--and critical of--the docile horde."

Although she experienced theory as a mode of rebellion, she had also, like me,
first been initiated into it by her academic family. On this front, Eakin's
theory pedigree is more impressive than mine. She spent part of her childhood
at its Ground Zero--Paris--while her parents were on sabbatical there; she
recounts her mother picking her up late from preschool after attending a
lecture by Claude Levi-Strauss. Eakin then attended Harvard at the peak of
theory's 1980s vogue, and studied with some of its leading American acolytes.

By the time I arrived at graduate school in the mid-aughts, theory was still
very much in the air, but its novelty had worn off; it had become, in a phrase
Eakin quotes from the literary scholar Nicholas Dames, "part of the furniture
of our lives." By then, mainstream culture, which had once found the theorists
titillating enough to dedicate cover articles and magazine spreads to their
antics, had wearied of them. Not long before I enrolled in doctoral studies,
Eakin was working on the ideas beat at _The New York Times_ when the paper
published an infamous contemptuous obituary of Derrida, the headline of which
dismissed the philosopher as an "abstruse theorist." In her penultimate
chapter, she confesses that she was consulted by the obit's editor before
publication and--to her apparent regret--signed off on it.

Around the same time, Eakin also reported for the _Times_ on a symposium on
"the future of theory" convened by the leading journal _Critical Inquiry_. The
illustrious participants, she discovered, sounded "despondent about the value
of their work." The headline for her write-up of the event captured the
desultory mood: "The Latest Theory Is that Theory Doesn't Matter." The same
year, the British Marxist Terry Eagleton, whose primer _Literary Theory_ has
initiated generations of students, published a book called _After Theory_ , a
sort of obituary for French Theory writ large. What exactly was supposed to
come next was anyone's guess. During my grad school years, that situation
provoked no end of anxiety for aspiring scholars hoping to place the right bet
on the next big paradigm and reap the requisite grants and ever-scarcer
tenure-track jobs.

But Eakin wants to argue that reports of theory's death--including the one she
penned back in 2003--were greatly exaggerated. The _Critical Inquiry_
panelists, she says near the end of _The Frenchmen_ , "were wrong" to dismiss
theory's relevance; today, she imagines, "most of them would agree." One area
of renewed pertinence, she notes, is the rise of Large Language Models, which
seem to operationalize a key French Theory idea: that language is an
autonomous system that can function without a human subject. In 1967, Roland
Barthes proclaimed "The Death of the Author," declaring that "to write" is "to
reach that point where only language acts, 'performs,' and not 'me.'" As Eakin
notes, Barthes "anticipated the production of texts without authors." Once
counterintuitive, such provocations are now anything but.

> "Once counterintuitive, such provocations are now anything but."

This uncanny technological ratification of theory--as well as various other
ways that what was once intellectual scandal has become what some French
theorists called _doxa_ --raises as many questions as it resolves. Theory's
allure, as Eakin reveals with self-satirizing flair in her autobiographical
passages, was its oppositional, countercultural energy. So what becomes of it
when something resembling its agenda is being executed by the most highly
valued companies in the world; or, to name another example, when ideas drawn
from queer theory, derived from Foucault's critiques of "normalization," are
embraced by medical experts, state officials, and corporations? If theory's
core value, as Eakin tells us in the closing lines of the book, is "vigilant
questioning," what should be its inheritors' stance toward its current
institutionalized forms?

Despite her book's other virtues, Eakin's answer left me unsatisfied. To the
extent that she celebrates theory's conquest of common sense, she arguably
betrays the legacy of skepticism she otherwise endorses. Notably, in the final
chapter, she hails theory's "imprint on the revolution in gender pronouns,"
declaring: "The more fluid our language, the more capacious and less confined
our self-definitions, our bodies, our imaginations--and, eventually, the more
tolerant our social order." But any serious reader of Foucault, who
[_contended_](https://www.compactmag.com/article/why-foucault-couldnt-kill-
sexuality/) that what might look like the freeing up of sexuality turns out to
be its ensnarement in new discursive regimes, should surely be wary of the
ostensible liberation being heralded here. We needn't go into the intricacies
of Foucault's thought to wonder whether demands that we attach pronouns to our
public identities and identify our internally felt "gender identities" are in
fact ways of achieving a "less confined self-definition"--or the opposite.
Such matters, in any case, merit "vigilant questioning," but Eakin applauds
the fact that the answers are now "intuitive to Generation Z."

* * *

One Frenchman whose name never appears in Eakin's book is [_Ren e
Girard_](https://www.compactmag.com/article/rene-girard-and-the-rise-of-
victim-power/), and not for lack of opportunity to mention it. Girard was the
lead organizer of the 1966 Johns Hopkins symposium "The Languages of
Criticisms and the Sciences of Man," the watershed event that introduced
French Theory to American academia and the subject of a chapter in _The
Frenchmen_. Eakin even refers to the "enterprising trio of professors" who
organized the event, and goes on to name two of them, Richard Macksey and
Eugenio Donato, but not the most famous of the three. One of the sources cited
in the notes for the chapter on the Hopkins symposium is Cynthia Haven's 2018
biography of Girard. To use a phrase dear to Derrida, it is as if Girard has
been placed _sous rature_ ("under erasure"): He is present in _The Frenchmen_
only in his glaring absence.

Steeped as I am in French Theory's hermeneutic of suspicion, I can't help but
find something significant in this omission. My read on it connects to what I
take to be the most compelling and insightful sections of Eakin's book: the
ones that wittily recount her youthful seduction by theory, and the follies
and excesses to which that seduction led. In these sections, as well as some
of the biographical passages on the major theorists, the book shares some of
the panache of the comic novels that have engaged fruitfully with this subject
matter, from David Lodge's _Small World_ to Laurent Binet's _The Seventh
Function of Language_. Another such text and a frequent point of reference for
Eakin is Jeffrey Eugenides's _The Marriage Plot_ , a comedy of manners set at
Brown, the hotbed of American semiotics in the 1980s (and my own doctoral alma
mater a few decades later).

Eakin says her aim in retelling the theorists' story--filtered through the
story of her own infatuation with them--is to "re-embody these men" and
thereby to "recover the hidden human element beneath their often stringent
antihumanism." They pronounced the death of the author and the evanescence of
"Man," but much of their appeal derived from their--often assiduously
cultivated--individual idiosyncrasies. Eakin offers a vivid rendering of this
paradox, but doesn't quite account for it. One of her formulations, already
cited above, offers a hint: Theory, she thought in her youth, made you
"different from--and critical of--the docile horde." What more radical move of
self-differentiation from the crowd could there be than to enact a secession
from humanity itself?

> "Girard trained his own hermeneutic of suspicion on just this sort of
> gesture."

Girard trained his own hermeneutic of suspicion on just this sort of gesture.
His signature intellectual move was to show that beneath such ostentatious
efforts at self-differentiation, one could always find sameness, imitation,
envy, and jealousy--the studiously concealed workings of what he called
"mimetic desire." Without deploying Girard's concept, Eakin illustrates it
nicely at another point when she describes a phase in college when she modeled
herself after Nadja, the heroine of the surrealist Andre Breton's 1928 novel
of the same name and an icon of spontaneity and radical individual freedom.
But as she tried to remake herself in the image of Breton's "_g enie libre_,"
forcing herself to "do wild and impulsive things," Eakin found that she "began
to crack under the pressure." The fantasy of absolute spontaneity had led to
its opposite: slavish imitation.

For Girard, something like this predicament lies at the heart of modern
culture and explains many of its pathologies. Humans are fundamentally
imitative creatures, and in prior eras our mimetic impulses were governed by
preordained hierarchies, our role models were set for us, and our activities
were channeled into structured apprenticeships. Modernity abolished these
structures, elevating innovation over emulation, distinction over
assimilation, rupture over continuity--and yet its denizens had never ceased
to imitate. Avant-garde artists and intellectuals thus become caught up in a
"mad escalation" as the pursuit of originality leads them to ever greater
mimetic enslavement, which they must deny ever more vigorously.

When she observes of her theory-smitten cohort at Harvard: "That we were
hardly as original or as special or as independent-minded as we thought didn't
occur to us"; or when she recounts the bitter intellectual feuds that pitted
Derrida against his former teacher Foucault, Derrida against Lacan, Lacan
against his wayward disciple Felix Guattari, and so on, Eakin stumbles upon
this insight of Girard's. French theorists' pursuit of individuality led them
to dissolve the notion of the individual, but their antihuman philosophy was
symptomatic of the all-too-human status competition in which they were deeply
invested. That Eakin reveals all of this in narrative form vindicates another
Girardian idea: that it is often novelists who manage to disclose what
intellectuals take pains to conceal.

Eakin concludes _The Frenchmen_ by affirming a soft version of theory's
mantras: "Be skeptical. Be alert. Pay very close attention. Beware political
claims posing as timeless truths." The passages about her youthful excesses,
though, suggest we should also be skeptical of this ethos of constant
intellectual self-differentiation through skepticism, because where it tends
to lead is to a susceptibility to superficial intellectual fashions. Moreover,
if, as Eakin says, theory has become something like the common sense of our
culture, our wariness should surely be directed, not least, at its own deeper
presuppositions. But the problem, as Girard helps us see, is that such
skepticism also risks becoming subject to the same perverse mimetic dynamics
as what it opposes. That is what has occurred with the self-defeating
[_absurdities_](https://compactmag.substack.com/p/right-wing-victim-
power?ref=compactmag.com) of today's countercultural right, whose struggles
against "wokeness" have led it to
[_reproduce_](https://compactmag.substack.com/p/welcome-to-the-bizarro-
awokening?ref=compactmag.com) all of the major "woke" pathologies.

"Theory's legacy of vigilant questioning, of scrupulous attentiveness to
language's complexities and contradictions," Eakin writes, "is not
antithetical to the common good." But how do we define the common good when
the sources of a shared culture have been so severely eroded? The question
becomes more urgent by the day, as AI's automation of culture propels us into
a post-literate state. On this front, I'm afraid that despite the prescience
of many of their ideas, Eakin's and my beloved theorists offer little
guidance. Their imperative--to deconstruct--has been followed all too
faithfully, for too long. If we need anything today, it is to construct.
